title: Growing coriander microgreens
subtitle: Slow herb microgreens with a distinctive citrus-soap flavour, cut in 14 to 21 days
excerpt: Coriander microgreens are one of the more challenging herb microgreens to grow: the seed has a thick husk that slows germination, and the cycle is 14 to 21 days. The cotyledons have a concentrated citrus-forward coriander flavour.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Rinsing seed before sowing to remove dust, seed-treatment residues, and surface sugars that can encourage mould on microgreen trays. Standard practice for coriander, where the double-hulled seed benefits from soaking and rinsing to soften the outer coat before sowing.

A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

content.text: Coriander microgreens are a year-round indoor tray crop that takes 14 to 21 days from sowing to cut. The coriander fruit (what is commonly called the seed) is a double-hulled round ball containing two seeds; the outer hull can slow germination significantly. Soaking overnight and lightly cracking the husk before sowing improves germination rates. The cotyledons have a concentrated citrus-forward coriander flavour.
Coriander is slower and slightly less reliable than brassica microgreens but the flavour pay-off is high for coriander fans. Expect some variation in germination even from fresh seed.

Light: a bright south-facing windowsill in spring and summer. In winter, a grow light at 14 to 16 hours per day, 15 to 20 cm above the tray, is recommended. Coriander microgreens in low light become elongated and pale.
Temperature: 18 to 22°C. Coriander germinates best in warmth; below 15°C germination is very slow and unreliable. A heated propagator for the germination phase improves success rates in winter.
Night before day 0: prepare the seed.

and soaking: soak coriander seed in room-temperature water for 8 to 12 hours. After soaking, drain and place a small batch between two sheets of paper and roll gently with a rolling pin to crack the outer hull without splitting the inner seed. Rinse again before sowing. This step significantly improves germination rates.
Day 0: sow. Fill the tray with pre-dampened seed compost to within 1 cm of the rim. Scatter coriander seed at 15 to 20 g per 25 cm tray. Press gently into contact with the medium.

Days 1 to 5: blackout. Cover with a second tray, lightly weighted. Coriander germinates more slowly than brassicas; the blackout phase runs four to five days. Remove when most shoots are upright at 2 to 3 cm.
Day 6 onward: light. Bottom-water daily. Coriander cotyledons green up over 24 to 48 hours in bright light. Allow 14 to 21 days total for the cotyledons to fully develop.

Days 14 to 21: cut. Cut 1 cm above the medium when cotyledons are fully open and 5 to 8 cm tall. Use fresh; coriander microgreens wilt more quickly than brassica cotyledons. Refrigerate in a sealed container for up to one day.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common problems with coriander microgreen trays.

items.cause: Uncrushed outer hull, old seed, or cold room.
items.fix: Lightly crush the seed between sheets of paper before soaking on the next attempt. Use seed from the current season. Aim for room temperature above 18°C.

items.cause: Extended damp period over the long growing cycle.
items.fix: Bottom-water only. Run a small fan for airflow. The mould is on the substrate; the cotyledons are safe.

items.symptom: Cotyledons fail to develop past the folded seedling stage
items.fix: Move to a warmer, brighter position. Coriander needs both warmth and light to develop properly.

content.text: Use untreated coriander seed. Standard spice coriander (the whole round seed) works for microgreen growing; the twin seeds inside each hull usually germinate together. Crushing the hull before sowing is the most reliable way to improve germination rates.
risk is moderate over the extended cycle. Bottom-water only and maintain airflow throughout.
